claim: Standard statistical imputation approaches rely on the co-location of large whole-genome sequencing-based reference panels, powerful computing environments, and potentially sensitive genetic study data.
source: Standard statistical imputation approaches rely on the co-location of large whole-genome sequencing-based reference panels, powerful computing environments, and potentially sensitive genetic study data.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of current imputation approaches.

claim: Standard statistical imputation approaches result in computational resource and privacy-risk barriers to access to cutting-edge imputation techniques.
source: This results in computational resource and privacy-risk barriers to access to cutting-edge imputation techniques.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the requirements of standard approaches.

claim: The accuracy of current statistical approaches is known to degrade in regions of low and complex linkage disequilibrium.
source: Moreover, the accuracy of current statistical approaches is known to degrade in regions of low and complex linkage disequilibrium.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of current methods.

claim: Artificial neural network-based imputation approaches may overcome limitations of statistical approaches by encoding complex genotype relationships in easily portable inference models.
source: Artificial neural network-based imputation approaches may overcome these limitations by encoding complex genotype relationships in easily portable inference models.
evidence: This is stated as a potential advantage of neural network approaches.

claim: The autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy achieved superior imputation accuracy across the allele-frequency spectrum.
source: Our autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy achieved superior imputation accuracy across the allele-frequency spectrum and across genomes of diverse ancestry, while delivering at least fourfold faster inference run time relative to standard imputation tools.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: The autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy achieved superior imputation accuracy across genomes of diverse ancestry.
source: Our autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy achieved superior imputation accuracy across the allele-frequency spectrum and across genomes of diverse ancestry, while delivering at least fourfold faster inference run time relative to standard imputation tools.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: The autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy delivered at least fourfold faster inference run time relative to standard imputation tools.
source: Our autoencoder-based genotype imputation strategy achieved superior imputation accuracy across the allele-frequency spectrum and across genomes of diverse ancestry, while delivering at least fourfold faster inference run time relative to standard imputation tools.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: The human genome is inherited in large blocks from parental genomes, generated through a DNA-sequence-dependent shuffling process called recombination.
source: The human genome is inherited in large blocks from parental genomes, generated through a DNA-sequence-dependent shuffling process called recombination.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about genome inheritance.

claim: The non-uniform nature of recombination breakpoints results in correlative genotype relationships across genetic variants, known as linkage disequilibrium.
source: The non-uniform nature of recombination breakpoints producing these genomic blocks results in correlative genotype relationships across genetic variants, known as linkage disequilibrium.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about linkage disequilibrium.

claim: Genotypes for a small subset (1–10%) of observed common genetic variants can be used to infer the genotype status of unobserved but known genetic variation sites across the genome (on the order of ~1 M of >10 M sites).
source: Thus, genotypes for a small subset (1–10%) of observed common genetic variants can be used to infer the genotype status of unobserved but known genetic variation sites across the genome (on the order of ~1 M of >10 M sites; Li et al., 2009; Marchini and Howie, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Genotype imputation allows for the generation of nearly the full complement of known common genetic variation at a fraction of the cost of direct genotyping or sequencing.
source: This process, called genotype imputation, allows for the generation of nearly the full complement of known common genetic variation at a fraction of the cost of direct genotyping or sequencing.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of genotype imputation.

claim: Genotype imputation is an essential approach in population genetics.
source: Given the massive scale of genotyping required for genome-wide association studies or implementation of genetically informed population health initiatives, genotype imputation is an essential approach in population genetics.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the importance of imputation.

claim: Standard approaches to genotype imputation utilize Hidden Markov Models (HMM) distributed alongside large WGS-based reference panels.
source: Standard approaches to genotype imputation utilize Hidden Markov Models (HMM) (Browning et al., 2018; Das et al., 2016; Rubinacci et al., 2020) distributed alongside large WGS-based reference panels (Browning and Browning, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: HMM-based imputation algorithms use genetic variants shared between to-be-imputed genomes and the reference panel and apply Hidden Markov Models to impute the missing genotypes per sample.
source: In general terms, these imputation algorithms use genetic variants shared between to-be-imputed genomes and the reference panel and apply Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to impute the missing genotypes per sample (Das et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The hidden states in HMMs represent the haplotype in a reference panel that is most closely related to the haplotype being imputed.
source: The hidden states in the HMMs represent the haplotype in a reference panel that is most closely related to the haplotype being imputed.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation of HMM methodology.

claim: HMM parameter estimation depends on recombination rates, mutation rates, and/or genotype error rates that must be fit by Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithm (MCMC) or an expectation-maximization algorithm.
source: The HMM parameter estimation also depends on recombination rates, mutation rates, and/or genotype error rates that must be fit by Markov Chain Monte Carlo Algorithm (MCMC) or an expectation-maximization algorithm.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of HMM-based imputation.

claim: HMM-based imputation is a computationally intensive process, requiring access to both high-performance computing environments and large, privacy-sensitive, WGS reference panels.
source: Thus, HMM-based imputation is a computationally intensive process, requiring access to both high-performance computing environments and large, privacy-sensitive, WGS reference panels (Kowalski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Investigators outside of large consortia often resort to submitting genotype data to imputation servers, resulting in privacy and scalability concerns.
source: Often, investigators outside of large consortia will resort to submitting genotype data to imputation servers (Das et al., 2016), resulting in privacy and scalability concerns (Sarkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Autoencoders have attracted attention in functional genomics for their ability to fill-in missing data for image restoration and inpainting.
source: Recently, artificial neural networks, especially autoencoders, have attracted attention in functional genomics for their ability to fill-in missing data for image restoration and inpainting (Chaitanya et al., 2017; Ghosh et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Autoencoders are neural networks tasked with reconstructing the original input data, with constraints applied to achieve goals like dimensionality reduction or de-noising.
source: Autoencoders are neural networks tasked with the problem of simply reconstructing the original input data, with constraints applied to the network architecture or transformations applied to the input data in order to achieve a desired goal like dimensionality reduction or compression, and de-noising or de-masking (Abouzid et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Voulodimos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Stochastic noise or masking is used to modify or remove data inputs, training the autoencoder to reconstruct the original uncorrupted data from corrupted inputs.
source: Stochastic noise or masking is used to modify or remove data inputs, training the autoencoder to reconstruct the original uncorrupted data from corrupted inputs (Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Autoencoders that receive corrupted or masked data as input and are trained to predict the original uncorrupted data as the output are known as denoising autoencoders.
source: Autoencoders that receive corrupted or masked data as input and are trained to predict the original uncorrupted data as the output are also known as denoising autoencoders.
evidence: This is stated as a definition.

claim: Autoencoder characteristics are well-suited for genotype imputation and may address some of the limitations of HMM-based imputation by eliminating the need for dissemination of reference panels and allowing the capture of non-linear relationships in genomic regions with complex linkage disequilibrium structures.
source: These autoencoder characteristics are well-suited for genotype imputation and may address some of the limitations of HMM-based imputation by eliminating the need for dissemination of reference panels and allowing the capture of non-linear relationships in genomic regions with complex linkage disequilibrium structures.
evidence: This is stated as a potential advantage of autoencoders.

claim: Some attempts at genotype imputation using neural networks have been previously reported for specific genomic contexts at genotype masking levels (5–20%) not applicable in typical real-world population genetics scenarios.
source: Some attempts at genotype imputation using neural networks have been previously reported, though for specific genomic contexts (Naito et al., 2021) at genotype masking levels (5–20%) not applicable in typical real-world population genetics scenarios (Chen and Shi, 2019; Islam et al., 2021; Sun and Kardia, 2008), or in contexts where the neural network must be trained for imputation with specific input variant sets, i.e. the model must be re-trained for imputation from different genotyping array (Kojima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The study presents a generalized approach to unphased human genotype imputation using sparse, denoising autoencoders capable of highly accurate genotype imputation at genotype masking levels (98+%) appropriate for array-based genotyping and low-pass sequencing-based population genetics initiatives.
source: Here, we present a generalized approach to unphased human genotype imputation using sparse, denoising autoencoders capable of highly accurate genotype imputation at genotype masking levels (98+%) appropriate for array-based genotyping and low-pass sequencing-based population genetics initiatives.
evidence: This is stated as the main contribution of the study.

claim: The study describes the initial training and implementation of autoencoders spanning all of human chromosome 22, achieving equivalent to superior accuracy relative to modern HMM-based methods.
source: We describe the initial training and implementation of autoencoders spanning all of human chromosome 22, achieving equivalent to superior accuracy relative to modern HMM-based methods, and dramatically improving computational efficiency at deployment without the need to distribute reference panels.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding.

claim: The autoencoder approach dramatically improves computational efficiency at deployment without the need to distribute reference panels.
source: We describe the initial training and implementation of autoencoders spanning all of human chromosome 22, achieving equivalent to superior accuracy relative to modern HMM-based methods, and dramatically improving computational efficiency at deployment without the need to distribute reference panels.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding.

claim: Sparse, de-noising autoencoders spanning all bi-allelic SNPs observed in the Haplotype Reference Consortium were developed and optimized.
source: Sparse, de-noising autoencoders spanning all bi-allelic SNPs observed in the Haplotype Reference Consortium were developed and optimized.
evidence: This is stated in the Overview section of Materials and methods.

claim: Each autoencoder receives masked data as input and is trained to predict the original uncorrupted data as the output.
source: Each autoencoder receives masked data as input and is trained to predict the original uncorrupted data as the output.
evidence: This is stated in the Overview section of Materials and methods.

claim: Each bi-allelic SNP was encoded as two binary input nodes, representing the presence or absence of each allele.
source: Each bi-allelic SNP was encoded as two binary input nodes, representing the presence or absence of each allele (Figure 1B, E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B and E.

claim: The encoding allows for the straightforward extension to multi-allelic architectures and non-binary allele presence probabilities.
source: This encoding allows for the straightforward extension to multi-allelic architectures and non-binary allele presence probabilities.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the encoding approach.

claim: A data augmentation approach using modeled recombination events and offspring formation coupled with random masking at an escalating rate drove the autoencoder training strategy.
source: A data augmentation approach using modeled recombination events and offspring formation coupled with random masking at an escalating rate drove our autoencoder training strategy (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: A focal-loss-based approach was essential to genotype imputation performance due to the extreme skew of the allele frequency distribution for rarely present alleles.
source: Because of the extreme skew of the allele frequency distribution for rarely present alleles (Auton et al., 2015), a focal-loss-based approach was essential to genotype imputation performance.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Individual autoencoders were designed to span genomic segments with boundaries defined by computationally identified recombination hotspots.
source: Individual autoencoders were designed to span genomic segments with boundaries defined by computationally identified recombination hotspots (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The starting point for model hyperparameters were randomly selected from a grid of possible combinations and were further tuned from a battery of features describing the complexity of the linkage-disequilibrium structure of each genomic segment.
source: The starting point for model hyperparameters were randomly selected from a grid of possible combinations and were further tuned from a battery of features describing the complexity of the linkage-disequilibrium structure of each genomic segment.
evidence: This is stated as the hyperparameter optimization strategy.

claim: Whole-genome sequence data from the Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC) was used for training and as the reference panel for comparison to HMM-based imputation.
source: Whole-genome sequence data from the Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC) was used for training and as the reference panel for comparison to HMM-based imputation (McCarthy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The HRC dataset consists of 27,165 samples and 39,235,157 biallelic SNPs generated using whole-genome sequence data from 20 studies of predominantly European ancestry.
source: The dataset consists of 27,165 samples and 39,235,157 biallelic SNPs generated using whole-genome sequence data from 20 studies of predominantly European ancestry (HRC Release 1.1): 83.92% European, 2.33% East Asian, 1.63% Native American, 2.17% South Asian, 2.96% African, and 6.99% admixed ancestry individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the training dataset.

claim: Genotype imputation autoencoders were trained for all 510,442 unique SNPs observed in HRC on human chromosome 22.
source: Genotype imputation autoencoders were trained for all 510,442 unique SNPs observed in HRC on human chromosome 22.
evidence: This is stated as the scope of the training.

claim: A balanced (50%:50% European and African genetic ancestry) subset of 796 whole genome sequences from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities cohort (ARIC) was used for model validation and selection.
source: A balanced (50%:50% European and African genetic ancestry) subset of 796 whole genome sequences from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities cohort (ARIC) (Mou et al., 2018), was used for model validation and selection.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The Wellderly, Human Genome Diversity Panel (HGDP), and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohorts were used for model testing.
source: The Wellderly (Erikson et al., 2016), Human Genome Diversity Panel (HGDP) (Cann et al., 2002), and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) (Bild et al., 2002 ) cohorts were used for model testing.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Wellderly cohort consisted of 961 whole genomes of predominantly European genetic ancestry.
source: The Wellderly cohort consisted of 961 whole genomes of predominantly European genetic ancestry.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the test dataset.

claim: HGDP consisted of 929 individuals across multiple ancestries: 11.84% European, 14.64% East Asian, 6.57% Native American, 10.98% African, and 55.97% admixed.
source: HGDP consisted of 929 individuals across multiple ancestries: 11.84% European, 14.64% East Asian, 6.57% Native American, 10.98% African, and 55.97% admixed.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the test dataset.

claim: MESA consisted of 5370 whole genomes across multiple ancestries: 27.62% European, 11.25% East Asian, 4.99% Native American, 5.53% African, and 50.61% admixed.
source: MESA consisted of 5370 whole genomes across multiple ancestries: 27.62% European, 11.25% East Asian, 4.99% Native American, 5.53% African, and 50.61% admixed.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the test dataset.

claim: MESA, Wellderly, and HGDP are all independent datasets, not used for autoencoder training, nor model selection.
source: MESA, Wellderly, and HGDP are all independent datasets, not used for autoencoder training, nor model selection, whereas HRC and ARIC were utilized for training and model selection, respectively.
evidence: This is stated to clarify the independence of test datasets.

claim: Random masking of input genotypes was performed at escalating rates during training, starting with a relatively low masking rate (80% of variants) that is gradually incremented until up to only five variants remain unmasked per autoencoder.
source: During training, random masking of input genotypes was performed at escalating rates, starting with a relatively low masking rate (80% of variants) that is gradually incremented in subsequent training rounds until up to only five variants remain unmasked per autoencoder.
evidence: This is stated as part of the training methodology.

claim: A total of 30,000 offspring genomes were generated using sim1000G and merged with the original HRC dataset for a total of 57,165 genomes during finetuning.
source: During finetuning we used sim1000G (Dimitromanolakis et al., 2019) to simulate of offspring formation using the default genetic map and HRC genomes as parents. A total of 30,000 offspring genomes were generated and merged with the original HRC dataset, for a total of 57,165 genomes.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The accuracy of allele presence reconstruction was scored using an adapted version of focal loss to account for the overwhelming abundance of rare variants.
source: In order to account for the overwhelming abundance of rare variants, the accuracy of allele presence reconstruction was scored using an adapted version of focal loss (FL) (Lin et al., 2017), shown in Equation 2.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The tiling process resulted in 256 genomic segments spanning chromosome 22: 188 independent LD segments, 32 high LD segments resulting from internal local minima splits, and 36 segments further split due to GPU memory limitations.
source: This tiling process resulted in 256 genomic segments spanning chromosome 22: 188 independent LD segments, 32 high LD segments resulting from internal local minima splits, and 36 segments further split due to GPU memory limitations.
evidence: This is stated as the result of the genome tiling process.

claim: A random grid search approach was used to define initial hyperparameter combinations producing generally accurate genotype imputation results.
source: We first used a random grid search approach to define initial hyperparameter combinations producing generally accurate genotype imputation results.
evidence: This is stated as the hyperparameter initialization strategy.

claim: The coarse-grain grid search was performed on all genomic segments of chromosome 22 (256 genomic segments), each tested with 100 randomly selected hyperparameter combinations per genomic segment.
source: This coarse-grain grid search was performed on all genomic segments of chromosome 22 (256 genomic segments), each tested with 100 randomly selected hyperparameter combinations per genomic segment, with a batch size of 256 samples, training for 500 epochs without any stop criteria, and validating on an independent dataset (ARIC).
evidence: This is stated as the grid search methodology.

claim: An ensemble-based machine learning approach (Extreme Gradient Boosting–XGBoost) was used to predict the expected performance (r-squared) of each hyperparameter combination per genomic segment.
source: In order to avoid local optimal solutions and reduce the hyperparameter search space, we used an ensemble-based machine learning approach (Extreme Gradient Boosting–XGBoost) to predict the expected performance (r-squared) of each hyperparameter combination per genomic segment using the results of the coarse-grid search and predictive features calculated for each genomic segment.
evidence: This is stated as the hyperparameter tuning strategy.

claim: The observed accuracies of the coarse-grid search, numbering 25,600 training inputs, were used to predict the accuracy of 500,000 new hyperparameter combinations.
source: The observed accuracies of the coarse-grid search, numbering 25,600 training inputs, were used to predict the accuracy of 500,000 new hyperparameter combinations selected from Table 1 without training.
evidence: This is stated as the scale of the hyperparameter prediction.

claim: The top 10 candidates per genomic segment along with the single best initially tested hyperparameter combination per genomic segments were selected for further consideration.
source: We then ranked all hyperparameter combinations by their predicted performance and selected the top 10 candidates per genomic segment along with the single best initially tested hyperparameter combination per genomic segments for further consideration.
evidence: This is stated as the hyperparameter selection strategy.

claim: Performance was compared to Minimac4, Beagle5, and Impute5 using default parameters.
source: Performance was compared to Minimac4 (Das et al., 2016), Beagle5 (Browning et al., 2018), and Impute5 (Rubinacci et al., 2020) using default parameters.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: HRC was utilized as reference panel for the HMM-based imputation tools, which is the same dataset used for training the autoencoders.
source: We utilized HRC as reference panel for the HMM-based imputation tools, which is the same dataset used for training the autoencoders, and we applied the same quality control standards for both HMM-based and autoencoder-based imputation.
evidence: This is stated to ensure fair comparison.

claim: Population level reconstruction accuracy is quantified by measuring r-squared across multiple strata of data.
source: Population level reconstruction accuracy is quantified by measuring r-squared across multiple strata of data: per genomic segment, at whole chromosome level, and stratified across multiple minor allele frequency bins: [0.001–0.005], [0.005–0.01], [0.01–0.05], [0.05–0.1], [0.1–0.2], [0.2–0.3], [0.3–0.4], [0.4–0.5].
evidence: This is stated as the accuracy measurement approach.

claim: Untuned autoencoder performance was generally inferior to all tested HMM-based methods except when tested on the European ancestry-rich Wellderly dataset when masked using the Affymetrix 6.0 and UKB Axiom marker sets, but not Omni 1.5 M markers.
source: Untuned autoencoder performance was generally inferior to all tested HMM-based methods except when tested on the European ancestry-rich Wellderly dataset when masked using the Affymetrix 6.0 and UKB Axiom marker sets, but not Omni 1.5 M markers.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the preliminary comparison.

claim: HMM-based imputation was consistently superior across the more ancestrally diverse test datasets (MESA and HGDP) before tuning.
source: HMM-based imputation was consistently superior across the more ancestrally diverse test datasets (MESA and HGDP) (two proportion test, p≤8.77 × 10–6).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: When performance across genomic segments, test datasets, and test array marker sets was combined, the untuned autoencoders exhibited an average r-squared per variant of 0.352±0.008 versus 0.374±0.007, 0.364±0.007, and 0.357±0.007 for Minimac4, Beagle5, and Impute5, respectively.
source: Overall, when performance across genomic segments, test datasets, and test array marker sets was combined, the autoencoders exhibited an average r-squared per variant of 0.352±0.008 in reconstruction of WGS ground truth genotypes versus an average r-squared per variant of 0.374±0.007, 0.364±0.007, and 0.357±0.007 for HMM-based imputation methods (Minimac4, Beagle5, and Impute5, respectively) (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to Table 2.

claim: The difference in performance between untuned autoencoders and HMM-based methods was statistically significant only relative to Minimac4.
source: This difference was statistically significant only relative to Minimac4 (Minimac4: Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.037, Beagle5 and Eagle5: p≥0.66).
evidence: This is stated as a statistical result.

claim: The autoencoder had superior performance when applied to genomic segments with the most complex LD structures: those with larger numbers of observed unique haplotypes, unique diplotypes, and heterozygosity, as well as high average MAF, and low average pairwise Pearson correlation across all SNPs.
source: We observed that the autoencoder had superior performance when applied to the genomic segments with the most complex LD structures: those with larger numbers of observed unique haplotypes, unique diplotypes, and heterozygosity, as well as high average MAF, and low average pairwise Pearson correlation across all SNPs (average LD) (Spearman correlation ρ≥0.22, p≤9.8 × 10–04).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: Superior autoencoder performance was associated with a low proportion explained by the first two principal components and positively correlated with the number of components required to explained 90% of variance.
source: Concordantly, superior autoencoder performance was associated with a low proportion explained by the first two components and positively correlated with the number of components required to explained 90% of variance (Spearman ρ≥0.22, p≤8.3 × 10–04).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: An ensemble model inference approach was able to predict the genomic segment-specific performance of hyperparameter combinations with high accuracy (mean r-squared=0.935 ± 0.002 of predicted vs observed autoencoders accuracies via 10-fold cross validation).
source: An ensemble model inference approach was able to predict the genomic segment-specific performance of hyperparameter combinations with high accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, mean r-squared=0.935 ± 0.002 of predicted vs observed autoencoders accuracies via 10-fold cross validation).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: After tuning, autoencoder performance surpassed HMM-based imputation performance across all imputation methods, independent test datasets, and genotyping array marker sets.
source: After tuning, autoencoder performance surpassed HMM-based imputation performance across all imputation methods, independent test datasets, and genotyping array marker sets.
evidence: This is stated as a main result.

claim: At a minimum, autoencoders surpassed HMM-based imputation performance in >62% of chromosome 22 genomic segments after tuning.
source: At a minimum, autoencoders surpassed HMM-based imputation performance in >62% of chromosome 22 genomic segments (two proportion test p=1.02 × 10–11) (Minimac4: Figure 3, Beagle5 and Eagle5: Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance and reference to figures.

claim: The optimized autoencoders exhibited superior performance with an average r-squared of 0.395±0.007 vs 0.374±0.007 for Minimac4, 0.364±0.007 for Beagle5, and 0.358±0.007 for Impute5.
source: Overall, the optimized autoencoders exhibited superior performance with an average r-squared of 0.395±0.007 vs 0.374±0.007 for Minimac4 (Wilcoxon rank sum test p=0.007), 0.364±0.007 for Beagle5 (Wilcoxon rank sum test p=1.53*10–4), and 0.358±0.007 for Impute5 (Wilcoxon rank sum test p=2.01*10–5) (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance and reference to Table 4.

claim: The superiority of autoencoders was robust to the marker sets tested, with the mean r-squared per genomic segment for autoencoders being 0.373±0.008, 0.399±0.007, and 0.414±0.008 vs 0.352±0.008, 0.370±0.006, and 0.400±0.007 for Minimac4 using Affymetrix 6.0, UKB Axiom, and Omni 1.5 M marker sets.
source: This superiority was robust to the marker sets tested, with the mean r-squared per genomic segment for autoencoders being 0.373±0.008, 0.399±0.007, and 0.414±0.008 vs 0.352±0.008, 0.370±0.006, and 0.400±0.007 for Minimac4 using Affymetrix 6.0, UKB Axiom, and Omni 1.5 M marker sets (Wilcoxon rank-sums test P-value = 0.029, 1.99*10–4, and 0.087, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: Tuning improved performance of the autoencoders across all genomic segments, generally improving the superiority of autoencoders relative to HMM-based approaches in genomic segments with complex haplotype structures while equalizing performance relative to HMM-based approaches in genomic segments with more simple LD structures.
source: Tuning improved performance of the autoencoders across all genomic segments, generally improving the superiority of autoencoders relative to HMM-based approaches in genomic segments with complex haplotype structures while equalizing performance relative to HMM-based approaches in genomic segments with more simple LD structures (as described in Materials and methods, by the number of unique haplotypes: Figure 3—figure supplement 3, diplotypes: Figure 3—figure supplement 4, average pairwise LD: Figure 3—figure supplement 5, proportion variance explained: Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to multiple figure supplements.

claim: Use of the augmented reference panel did not improve HMM-based imputation, having no influence on Minimac4 performance.
source: Use of the augmented reference panel did not improve HMM-based imputation, having no influence on Minimac4 performance (original overall r-squared of 0.374±0.007 vs 0.363±0.007 after augmentation, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.0917), and significantly degrading performance of Beagle5 and Impute5 (original r-squared of 0.364±0.007 and 0.358±0.007 vs 0.349±0.006 and 0.324±0.007 after augmentation, p=0.026 and p=1.26*10–4, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: After merging the results from all genomic segments, the whole chromosome accuracy of autoencoder-based imputation remained superior to all HMM-based imputation tools, across all independent test datasets, and all genotyping array marker sets.
source: After merging the results from all genomic segments, the whole chromosome accuracy of autoencoder-based imputation remained superior to all HMM-based imputation tools, across all independent test datasets, and all genotyping array marker sets (Wilcoxon rank-sums test p≤5.55 × 10–67).
evidence: This is stated as a result with statistical significance.

claim: The autoencoder's mean r-squared per variant ranged from 0.363 for HGDP to 0.605 for the Wellderly vs 0.340–0.557 for Minimac4, 0.326–0.549 for Beagle5, and 0.314–0.547 for Eagle5 at the whole chromosome level.
source: The autoencoder's mean r-squared per variant ranged from 0.363 for HGDP to 0.605 for the Wellderly vs 0.340–0.557 for Minimac4, 0.326–0.549 for Beagle5, and 0.314–0.547 for Eagle5, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a result.

claim: When imputation accuracy is stratified by MAF bins, the autoencoders maintain superiority across all MAF bins by nearly all test dataset and genotyping array marker sets.
source: Further, when imputation accuracy is stratified by MAF bins, the autoencoders maintain superiority across all MAF bins by nearly all test dataset and genotyping array marker sets (Figure 4, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Autoencoder imputation accuracy is similarly superior when measured with F1-scores and concordance, though these metrics are less sensitive at capturing differences in rare variant imputation accuracy.
source: Concordantly, autoencoder imputation accuracy is similarly superior when measured with F1-scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and concordance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), though these metrics are less sensitive at capturing differences in rare variant imputation accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to figure supplements.

claim: When the reference panel of the HMM-based tools is upgraded to the more diverse TOPMed dataset, the HRC-trained autoencoder remains superior across all ancestry groups of HGDP.
source: Thus, with training on equivalent reference cohorts, autoencoder performance was superior across all variant allele frequencies and ancestries with the primary source of superiority arising from hard to impute regions with complex LD structures. When the reference panel of the HMM-based tools is upgraded to the more diverse TOPMed dataset, the HRC-trained autoencoder remains superior across all ancestry groups of HGDP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), as well as in the MESA ancestries well represented in HRC (European and East Asian) but not in MESA ancestries where representation is significantly enhanced by the TOPMed reference panel (American and African) with additional imputation performance deriving from a significant degree of familial relationships spanning the TOPMed reference panel and MESA test cohort (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to figure supplements.
